question: The 19th EU-Canada bilateral summit was held on 24 November 2023, with a view to forming a strategic partnership in the area of climate action. At that meeting, the President of the European Commission announced that the institution would finance, to the tune of EUR 600 million, the purchase of 12 new Canadian built planes (Canadairs) to increase the aerial firefighting capacity of rescEU.

A number of doubts have arisen over this operation. For one, it would involve reactivating the production line of an obsolete aircraft that has been out of production for nine years and whose safety certification, based on US standards dating back more than half a century, does not conform with EU standards.
For another, the contract with the private Canadian company for this EU-financed order has not been made publicly available. 1.

Could the Commission clarify whether technical due diligence has been carried out on the company before entering into this commitment, to check that it still has the required know-how, qualified staff, supply chain and certifications?

Could it clarify whether penalties are foreseen in case of delays, whether the aircraft still needs further development (if so, with what funding?) or whether the model already exists, and whether other alternatives have been assessed?
answer: The development of rescEU (1) firefighting assets stems from the identified need to boost the EU’s level of preparedness to respond to the devastating wildfires affecting Europe every summer. To support the Member States’ efforts, the Commission is financing the purchase of 12 firefighting aircraft through EU grants.

In line with the legal framework, the Commission, in consultation with the Member States, defined the quality requirements, such as the minimum water capacity and the minimum flying range, for the response capacities forming part of rescEU.

The purchase of the aircraft is subject to government-to-government agreements, with the Member States being the contracting authorities in accordance with their national legal framework and national procurement rules. The Commission cannot disclose information pertaining to contractual relationships between third parties. The Commission looks forward to strengthening the rescEU firefighting fleet without delay.
